pos: n. (proper name; a family of the tribe of Gad)
etymology: Hebrew 'Arodi, the family-name formed from Arod, a son of Gad. Genesis 46:16 spells the father Arodi; Numbers 26:17 spells him Arod and names the clan Arodites.
biblical_def: The Arodites are named once: “Of Arod, the family of the Arodites: of Areli, the family of the Arelites” (Numbers 26:17). The verse belongs to the second census, taken in the plains of Moab in the fortieth year, and the whole chapter is one of the most solemn pieces of bookkeeping in Scripture. The first census had been taken at Sinai; of the men counted there, not one remained alive but Caleb and Joshua. “For the LORD had said of them, They shall surely die in the wilderness” (Numbers 26:65). So the Arodites are enrolled in a list of the survivors of a judgment, the sons of men whose fathers' bodies lay behind them in the sand. The purpose of the count is given at verse 53: “Unto these the land shall be divided for an inheritance according to the number of names.” The numbering is not administrative curiosity; it is the register of who receives the promise. The Arodites were a small family in a middle-sized tribe, and their name is written down because the land was to be apportioned by name. God divides His inheritance to families He has counted, and a family too obscure for any other notice is counted here.

corruption_summary: Census lists are read as dry administrative residue; Numbers 26 is a register of inheritance taken after a judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: The numbered chapters of the Pentateuch are commonly skipped as bureaucratic deposit, and where they are studied they are often assigned to a priestly compiler with an interest in administration. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and reads the chapter as it presents itself: a count ordered by the LORD, taken at a named time and place, for a stated purpose. The purpose is inheritance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's promises are distributed by name. The land was not given to Israel in the abstract but divided among families enrolled in a book, and the New Testament keeps the figure: “your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). An inheritance apportioned by name is the comfort of every believer who has no standing of his own to plead.

pos: n. (proper name; a family of the tribe of Manasseh)
etymology: Hebrew 'Asri'eli, the family-name formed from Asriel, a descendant of Manasseh through Gilead. The personal name is generally read as containing 'el, God, with a first element of less certain sense.
biblical_def: The Asrielites are named once: “And of Asriel, the family of the Asrielites: and of Shechem, the family of the Shechemites” (Numbers 26:31). They are one of the six Gileadite families of Manasseh — the half-tribe whose inheritance would be split, half east of Jordan and half west. Manasseh was Joseph's firstborn, and the record of his line in Numbers 26 is unusual for how far down it reaches: the chapter names not only his sons but his grandsons' houses, and then, in the passage immediately following, the daughters of Zelophehad, whose petition for an inheritance in a tribe with no sons to carry it was granted by the LORD Himself (Numbers 27:1-7). So the tribe whose families are catalogued most minutely is the tribe through which Scripture establishes that a promise does not fail for want of a son to receive it. The Asrielites stand in that catalogue. Their name is one line in a chapter whose point is that the inheritance God swore to Abraham would reach every house entitled to it, down to the last family, and down to daughters when there were no sons.

corruption_summary: Detailed clan lists are read as evidence of a late scribal interest; here they are the legal basis of a land grant.
corruption_paragraphs: Manasseh's genealogy in Numbers 26 descends further than most, and the extra detail is usually credited to the interests of a later compiler. The simpler reading is the one the text gives: the families are listed because the land was divided among them by lot and by name, and a land grant requires exactly this kind of specificity. The chapter reads like a register because it is one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the precision of God's faithfulness. He did not promise Israel a country in general terms and leave the sorting to men. He named the families, fixed the lot, and then, when Zelophehad's daughters came with no brother to inherit, He gave judgment for them Himself. A promise that reaches that far down reaches far enough for any reader.

pos: n. (proper name; a family of the tribe of Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ashbeli, the family-name formed from Ashbel, the second son of Benjamin named at Genesis 46:21 and 1 Chronicles 8:1.
biblical_def: The Ashbelites appear once: “The sons of Benjamin after their families: of Bela, the family of the Belaites: of Ashbel, the family of the Ashbelites: of Ahiram, the family of the Ahiramites” (Numbers 26:38). Benjamin was the youngest of Jacob's twelve and the only one born in the land of promise, and his tribe would be the smallest, the most nearly destroyed, and the most remarkably preserved. The book of Judges closes with Benjamin reduced to six hundred men after the outrage at Gibeah — a tribe within a hair of extinction by its own sin and Israel's sword. Yet out of Benjamin came Israel's first king, and out of Benjamin came the apostle to the Gentiles, who named the tribe when he named himself: “of the tribe of Benjamin” (Romans 11:1). The Ashbelites are one of the houses that carried the tribe through. Their name survives in a census taken before any of that happened, which is the way the genealogies generally work: the families are enrolled, and only later does it become plain which thread God was keeping.

corruption_summary: Tribal lists are treated as retrojected fiction; Scripture uses them to show a preservation no tribe earned.
corruption_paragraphs: The twelve-tribe structure is widely handled as a later ideal imposed on a looser reality, with the family lists invented to fill it out. The dictionary holds the lists as record. The test is what the record then does with Benjamin: it tells of the tribe's near-annihilation by its own wickedness, which no inventor flattering a tribal ideal would supply.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is preserving grace. Benjamin was almost cut off and was kept, and the keeping was not for merit — the tribe's great hour in Judges is its shame. That God brought Saul and then Paul out of so nearly extinguished a house is the pattern of His dealing with all His people, who are preserved and not self-preserving.

pos: n. (proper name; a family of the tribe of Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Bal'i, the family-name formed from Bela, Benjamin's firstborn. The personal name is commonly connected with a root meaning to swallow up.
biblical_def: The Belaites are named once, heading the Benjamite families: “The sons of Benjamin after their families: of Bela, the family of the Belaites” (Numbers 26:38). Bela was Benjamin's firstborn (1 Chronicles 8:1), and his house therefore stands first in the roll. The Chronicler returns to this family more than once and traces it in some detail, for it was from Benjamin's line that the first king of Israel came, and the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8 and 9 are plainly concerned to establish Saul's descent. There is a quiet lesson in the placement. Bela stands first by birth, and his house is given the first line of the census; and yet the tribe's whole significance in redemptive history turns not on precedence but on God's free choosing — a king out of the smallest tribe, and an apostle out of the tribe that had nearly ceased to be. The Belaites keep the first place that belonged to them, and they do not keep it by right of anything but birth order, which in Scripture confers a position in a list and settles nothing before God.

corruption_paragraphs: Ancient lists are often read as simple charters of privilege, with the firstborn's place in a roll taken to establish standing. The Belaites head the Benjamite families by birth, and Scripture records it without making anything of it. The same book that puts Bela first is the book in which Jacob displaces Esau, Ephraim displaces Manasseh, and David is fetched from behind the sheep.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that position in the record is not standing before God. The census gives the Belaites a first line and an inheritance; it does not give them election. “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Romans 9:16).

pos: n. (proper name; a family of the tribe of Ephraim)
etymology: Hebrew Bakri, the family-name formed from Becher. The personal name is connected with a root for a firstborn or a young camel.
biblical_def: The Bachrites appear once: “These are the sons of Ephraim after their families: of Shuthelah, the family of the Shuthalhites: of Becher, the family of the Bachrites: of Tahan, the family of the Tahanites” (Numbers 26:35). Ephraim was Joseph's younger son, and the family that bore his name became the leading tribe of the northern kingdom — so dominant that the prophets use Ephraim as a name for Israel entire. That eminence was not his by birth. Jacob, blind and dying, crossed his hands over the heads of Joseph's boys and set his right hand on the younger, and when Joseph tried to correct him the old man refused: “his younger brother shall be greater than he” (Genesis 48:19). The Bachrites are one of three Ephraimite families counted in the plains of Moab, a small house in a tribe that had itself been small and was made great by a deliberate reversal. The census records the house; Genesis records the reason the house mattered. God put His hand on the younger, and the tribe that should have been second became first.

corruption_paragraphs: Ephraim's later dominance in the north is usually accounted for by territory, fertility and position on the trade routes. Those were the means. Scripture gives the cause three books earlier, in a bedroom at Goshen, when Jacob crossed his hands and would not be corrected. The historian may describe how Ephraim grew; the text says why.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's blessing follows His word and not the order of nature. Manasseh was the elder and Ephraim was set above him by a deliberate act, announced before either tribe existed. Every reader who has no natural claim on anything should mark how often Scripture puts the right hand on the younger.

pos: n. (proper name; a family of the tribe of Reuben)
etymology: Hebrew Karmi, the family-name formed from Carmi, a son of Reuben. The personal name is commonly connected with kerem, a vineyard.
biblical_def: The Carmites are named once: “Of Hezron, the family of the Hezronites: of Carmi, the family of the Carmites” (Numbers 26:6). They are one of four Reubenite families, and the tribe they belong to is the tribe of the forfeited birthright. Reuben was Jacob's firstborn and lost the pre-eminence by his own sin: “Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel” (Genesis 49:4), and the Chronicler states the transfer flatly — the birthright was given to the sons of Joseph. Reuben's census families are duly counted and duly given a portion east of Jordan, and the tribe never produces a judge, a king, or a prophet. Deborah's song asks after Reuben and finds great thoughts of heart and no men at the battle (Judges 5:15-16). The Carmites stand in the roll of a tribe that kept its inheritance and lost its leadership, and the distinction is worth a reader's attention. God does not take back the land He has promised; He does withhold the honour a man has despised. Reuben's portion was secure and Reuben's excellence was gone.

corruption_summary: Reuben's decline is read as the fading of a tribal confederation; Scripture names it as a birthright forfeited for sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Reuben's slide from first place is generally explained as the ordinary erosion of a frontier tribe exposed on the eastern side of Jordan. Scripture gives a moral cause and gives it twice, in Jacob's blessing and in the Chronicler's aside. The birthright was not mislaid; it was taken away for a named sin, and the record says so in the same sentence in which it calls Reuben the firstborn.

The principle to recover is that sin costs office even where grace keeps the inheritance. Reuben's families were counted and given their land; Reuben's pre-eminence was gone for good. A man may be in the covenant and disqualified from honour within it, which is the burden of Paul's warning that he kept his own body in subjection lest he himself be a castaway (1 Corinthians 9:27).

pos: n. (proper name; a family of the tribe of Zebulun)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eloni, the family-name formed from Elon, a son of Zebulun. The personal name is connected with 'elon, an oak or a terebinth.
biblical_def: The Elonites are named once: “Of the sons of Zebulun after their families: of Sered, the family of the Sardites: of Elon, the family of the Elonites: of Jahleel, the family of the Jahleelites” (Numbers 26:26). Zebulun was Leah's sixth son and Jacob's tenth, and the tribe drew a portion in the north, in the hill country and down toward the lake. Scripture says little of Zebulun in the histories, and then says something very great about the tribe's territory. Isaiah names the land of Zebulun as the first place the light would come: “the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali … in Galilee of the nations” (Isaiah 9:1), and Matthew quotes it of Christ's ministry at Capernaum (Matthew 4:13-16). Nazareth stood in Zebulun's allotment. The Elonites are a family in the tribe whose hills the Lord walked and whose villages first heard Him preach. The census that enrolled them for a portion of ground was enrolling them, as it turned out, for the ground on which the gospel would be first proclaimed.

corruption_paragraphs: Zebulun's northern allotment is routinely written off as marginal, and the Galilee of the Gospels with it — a provincial district far from where anything mattered. Isaiah had said otherwise seven centuries before, and Matthew cites him to show that Christ's choice of Capernaum was no accident of convenience but the fulfilling of a word.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints the ground as well as the hour. The land divided to Zebulun's families by lot in the plains of Moab was the land on which the Light of the world would open His mouth. A portion assigned by a cast lot in the fortieth year was being assigned by the God who had already written Isaiah 9.

pos: n. (proper name; a family of the tribe of Ephraim)
etymology: Hebrew 'Erani, the family-name formed from Eran, a son of Shuthelah. The personal name is of uncertain meaning; a connection with a root for watchfulness has been proposed.
biblical_def: The Eranites are named once, and the verse that names them is unusual: “And these are the sons of Shuthelah: of Eran, the family of the Eranites” (Numbers 26:36). The census ordinarily lists the sons of a tribal patriarch and stops; here it goes one generation further, appending a single sub-family of a single Ephraimite house. No reason is given. Ephraim, the tribe in question, was numbered at thirty and two thousand five hundred — the smallest count in the chapter save Manasseh's partner tribes, and smaller than it had been forty years before at Sinai. A tribe that had shrunk is enrolled with an extra line of detail. The dictionary does not pretend to know why, and resists the temptation to supply a reason the text withholds. What may be said is that the register descends to a family that would otherwise have no existence in Scripture at all. One clause in one verse is the whole of what is known of the Eranites, and it was enough to the Holy Ghost to write it down. God's books go further down than our interest in them does.

corruption_summary: Unexplained detail in a list is taken as a sign of clumsy compilation; it is more simply a record that goes deeper than we would.
corruption_paragraphs: An extra genealogical line with no stated purpose is standard evidence, in the critical handling of the Pentateuch, for multiple sources carelessly joined. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and is content to leave a detail unexplained. A register kept by a careful hand will contain entries whose occasion the later reader cannot recover; that is a mark of a real document, not of a bad one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of God's notice. The Eranites are known to exist because one clause records them. No act of theirs is remembered, no land is named as theirs, no man of the family is identified. They were counted, and being counted by God is the whole of what Scripture reports about them — which is more than the world will report about most men.

pos: n. (proper name; a family of the tribe of Gad)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eri, the family-name formed from Eri, a son of Gad. The personal name is commonly connected with a root meaning to watch or to be awake.
biblical_def: The Erites are named once: “Of Ozni, the family of the Oznites: of Eri, the family of the Erites” (Numbers 26:16). Eri is the fifth of Gad's seven sons in Genesis 46:16, and his family is enrolled with the rest in the plains of Moab. Gad's tribe asked Moses for the land east of Jordan, because the country suited their cattle, and Moses granted it on one hard condition: the men of Gad must cross over armed and fight at the head of Israel until every tribe had its inheritance, and only then return. “We will not return unto our houses, until the children of Israel have inherited every man his inheritance” (Numbers 32:18). They kept it. Joshua sent them home at the end with a blessing. The Erites belong to that tribe, and to that undertaking. There is a plain pattern for a man in it: a portion received early does not excuse a man from the war that secures his brethren's portion. Gad had his land first and fought longest, and Scripture records the bargain and the keeping of it with evident approval.

corruption_summary: The Transjordan settlement is read as tribal self-interest; Scripture records a bargain kept at cost for the brethren.
corruption_paragraphs: Gad's request for land east of Jordan is often treated as straightforward self-dealing, and Moses' anger in Numbers 32 is read as the whole of the Bible's verdict. But the chapter does not end at the rebuke. It ends with a sworn undertaking, and the book of Joshua records that the undertaking was performed and the men dismissed with a blessing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an inheritance already secured is a reason to fight for others, not an excuse to go home. The Gadites' wives and children were safe behind them while they crossed Jordan armed. A Christian whose own standing is settled is in exactly that position, and the Gadite answer is the right one: not until every man has his inheritance.

pos: n. (proper name; a people or district of northern Israel)
etymology: Hebrew Berim, of uncertain meaning and uncertain reference; possibly a district name, possibly a people. The Authorized Version renders it Berites at its single occurrence.
biblical_def: The Berites are named once, in the pursuit of Sheba the son of Bichri: “And he went through all the tribes of Israel unto Abel, and to Bethmaachah, and all the Berites: and they were gathered together, and went also after him” (2 Samuel 20:14). Sheba had raised the cry of revolt against David — “We have no part in David” (2 Samuel 20:1) — and Joab pursued him to the far north, to Abel of Bethmaachah, and besieged the city. What ended the rebellion was neither a battle nor a king's mercy but a wise woman on the wall, who asked Joab why he would swallow up a city that was a mother in Israel, and then had Sheba's head thrown over the wall to him. The Berites are the last-named of the regions Sheba passed through gathering men. They are a geographical footnote in a rebellion that collapsed over a parapet. The dictionary records the name and the uncertainty honestly: what the Berites were is not recoverable from Scripture, and the entry will not invent what the text does not supply.

scriptures: And he went through all the tribes of Israel unto Abel, and to Bethmaachah, and all the Berites: and they were gathered together, and went also after him.

And there happened to be there a man of Belial, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjamite: and he blew a trumpet, and said, We have no part in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: every man to his tents, O Israel.

And they came and besieged him in Abel of Bethmaachah, and they cast up a bank against the city, and it stood in the trench: and all the people that were with Joab battered the wall, to throw it down.
I am one of them that are peaceable and faithful in Israel: thou seekest to destroy a city and a mother in Israel: why wilt thou swallow up the inheritance of the LORD?
corruption_summary: Rebellion against the LORD's anointed is dressed as a grievance about representation; Scripture calls Sheba a man of Belial.
corruption_paragraphs: Sheba's slogan has a modern ring — no part, no inheritance, every man to his tents — and it is easy to read his revolt as a reasonable northern complaint about a southern king. The text forecloses that reading in its first clause. He is “a man of Belial” (2 Samuel 20:1), and his rising is against the man God had anointed. The grievance may have had colour; the rebellion had none.

The principle to recover is the honour due to lawful authority, and the wisdom that spares a city. The woman on the wall of Abel did not take Sheba's part, and she did not let Joab destroy the inheritance of the LORD either. She distinguished the rebel from the town, and so saved it. That is a model of discernment under pressure the church has frequent need of.
